questions.prompt: Why do automated contrast tools struggle to evaluate text over a photograph?

options.text: Photographs use color profiles that tools cannot read.
Images contain many varying pixels, so one local color measurement may not represent the whole word.
Automated tools are programmed to ignore all image files.
Text over photographs is strictly forbidden.

questions.explanation: A photograph varies in lightness across its surface, so checking one point does not guarantee every letter is legible.
questions.hint: Think about how a photograph changes from dark corners to bright spots.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Understand why tools report indeterminate results on images.

questions.prompt: What is a scrim in user interface design?

options.text: A tool used to measure precise contrast ratios.
A semi-transparent dark overlay placed between an image and text.
A type of heavily weighted font used for headlines.
An error state where text completely disappears.

questions.explanation: A scrim darkens the background image, creating a more stable boundary for light text.
questions.hint: It operates as an overlay that acts as a protective layer.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Apply protective overlays to secure text visibility.

questions.prompt: Why is a dynamic background image risky for text contrast?

options.text: It forces the text to change color randomly.
It drains the battery of mobile devices too quickly.
A passing score today might fail tomorrow if the image changes to something lighter.
It prevents users from scrolling the page.

questions.explanation: An unprotected text layer can become illegible if unpredictable background content changes.
questions.hint: Consider what happens when a dark image swaps to a bright image.
questions.testedLearningPoint: Recognize the risk of changing dynamic content.
